keyVerseText: And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias;
rootMeaning: The Greek word Ἀμών (Amṓn) originates from the Hebrew אָמוֹן (ʼÂmôwn), which carries the meaning of a "skilled workman" or "master workman." This root suggests not merely a personal name but a title or quality associated with craftsmanship and expertise. Understanding Amṓn in this light enriches the common English gloss of 'Amon' by highlighting a background of skill and mastery embedded in the name's heritage.
usageInScripture: The term Ἀμών appears twice in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'Amon.' It is used as a proper noun referring specifically to an Israelite individual, namely a king of Judah. This consistent usage as a personal name, without variation in translation, underscores its function as a historical and genealogical marker within Scripture, connecting the lineage of David as recorded in Matthew 1:10.
theologicalSignificance: The name Amṓn, rooted in the idea of a master craftsman, reminds believers that God sovereignly ordains history and leadership with purpose and skill. As a king of Judah, Amṓn's place in the genealogy of Christ reveals God's providential care in preserving the royal line through flawed but significant individuals. This highlights the faithfulness of God in working through human history and genealogy to bring forth the Messiah. Recognizing the meaning behind the name enriches our appreciation of God's craftsmanship in salvation history.
keyVerseReflection: Matthew 1:10 states, 'And Ezekias begat Manasses; and Manasses begat Amon; and Amon begat Josias,' situating Amṓn firmly within the Messianic lineage. The inclusion of Amṓn here emphasizes the continuity of God's covenant promises through successive generations of Israelite kings. The name itself, evoking mastery and skill, subtly points to God's skilled governance in orchestrating the ancestry of Jesus Christ, reinforcing the divine hand in the unfolding of redemptive history.
